claims.claim: Cheng asked whether regex search or a JSON highlighter could be clearly faster on the GPU, and the lab tests that on 100,000 generated JSON documents.

sources.label: lab/json-search README, the question
sources.quote: I was wondering if there's a point where regex search or json highlighter

claims.claim: For one document the highlighter takes 80 µs on the CPU executor, and a round trip to the GPU alone takes 0.6 ms or more, so one document is no case for a GPU.

sources.label: lab/json-search README, one document
sources.quote: a round trip to the GPU alone takes 0.6 ms or more

claims.claim: Every document runs the same operations and no document reads another one's values, which is why one GPU thread can take one document.

sources.label: lab/json-search README, independence of documents
sources.quote: every document runs the same operations, and no document reads another one's values

claims.claim: The document buffer lays out each document as 512 code points followed by the text's length, and one thread reads its own row.

sources.label: json-step.ts, buffer layout
sources.quote: `cellsPerDocument` is the layout of buffer 0: 512 code points, then the text's length.

claims.claim: Of the 100,000 documents, 89,943 are valid and 10,057 are broken, across sixteen defect kinds, each between 474 and 748 documents.

sources.label: lab/json-search README, the generated documents
sources.quote: 89,943 are valid and 10,057 are broken

sources.label: lab/json-search README, defect kinds
sources.quote: **16 defects**

claims.claim: The highlighter's step is 37 operations per position, plus 17 more to close the document, so a full 512-position row costs 18,961 operations.

sources.label: lab/json-search README, operations per step
sources.quote: | JSON highlighter | 37, 17 | 107 |

sources.label: lab/json-search README, operations per document
sources.quote: 17 operations instead of 2: 18,961 operations per document

claims.claim: Written once inside a loop over positions, the highlighter's shader is 107 statements and compiles in 0.04 s, against about 2 s when every position is written out.

sources.label: lab/json-search README, loop shader compile time
sources.quote: The highlighter's shader then compiles in 0.04 s

sources.label: lab/json-search README, statement count
sources.quote: | JSON highlighter | 37, 17 | 107 |

claims.claim: The first version, with every position written out, took about 2 s to compile.

sources.label: lab/json-search README, first stage
sources.quote: and the shader took about 2 s to compile

claims.claim: Across 100,000 documents, 18,961 operations per document makes about 1.9 billion operations in one pass, which is simple arithmetic and not a measured count.

sources.label: lab/json-search README, operations per document
sources.quote: 17 operations instead of 2: 18,961 operations per document

claims.claim: With the documents already on the GPU, the highlighter's pass over all 100,000 documents takes 2.2 ms when passes follow each other.

sources.label: lab/json-search README, highlighter pass
sources.quote: the highlighter's pass takes 2.2 ms and a search 4.5 to 5.2 ms

claims.claim: The same program as generated JavaScript takes about 2.1 s, extrapolated from 5,000 documents, and 8.4 to 9.2 s on the CPU executor; the GPU's values matched the CPU's, with 51.6 million values and 0 different.

sources.label: lab/json-search README, CPU times
sources.quote: 2.1 s, extrapolated from 5,000 documents, and 8.4 to 9.2 s, with every position written out

sources.label: lab/json-search README, executor time
sources.quote: takes 8.4 to 9.2 s on the executor and 2.1 s as generated JavaScript

sources.label: lab/json-search README, value comparison
sources.quote: 51.6 million values, 0 different

claims.claim: The measurements are for one Apple M5 Max through Metal in headless Chrome on generated documents, and the lab says another GPU or browser may differ.

sources.label: lab/json-search README, machine
sources.quote: may all differ on another GPU

sources.label: lab/json-search README, machine
sources.quote: One Apple M5 Max, one browser, headless.

claims.claim: The search's pattern is data: its automaton sits in cells beside the text, so a new pattern writes cells and changes no program.

sources.label: search-step.ts, header
sources.quote: its automaton and its character classes sit in cells, so a new pattern writes

claims.claim: A pattern has one state per character or class it reads, plus one: error has 6 states and connection reset has 17.

sources.label: lab/json-search README, states per pattern
sources.quote: A pattern has one state per character or class it reads, plus one

sources.label: lab/json-search README, example patterns
sources.quote: `error` has 6 and `connection reset` has 17

claims.claim: A pattern may use up to sixteen character classes and thirty-two class boundaries, at every state capacity.

sources.label: search-step.ts, capacities
sources.quote: How many character classes and class boundaries a pattern may have

sources.label: search-step.ts, capacities
sources.quote: export const classCapacity = 16

claims.claim: Each code point's class picks a transition matrix of zeros and ones, and each step multiplies that matrix by the zero-one state vector.

sources.label: data-program.ts, transition cells
sources.quote: transitions[c][s][t] is 1 when a step from state s reads a code point of class c

sources.label: search-step.ts, step
sources.quote: each step multiplies the code point's transition

claims.claim: A search step takes one table read per pair of states: 64 reads at 8 states and 1,024 at 32.

sources.label: lab/json-search README, table reads per step
sources.quote: A search step takes one table read per pair of states

claims.claim: The reverse pass, from the end of the text, sets reach[j][s] to 1 when some path from state s at position j reads at least one code point and ends accepting.

sources.label: search-step.ts, reverse pass
sources.quote: reach[j][s] is 1 when some path from state s at position j reads at

claims.claim: The forward pass, from the start, marks a code point as part of a match when a state is reached by the match in progress and also marked by the reverse pass.

sources.label: search-step.ts, forward pass
sources.quote: reached[j][s] is 1 when the match in progress has reached state s by position j

sources.label: search-step.ts, forward pass
sources.quote: Code point j continues the match when reached[j][s] && reach[j][s] for some state s

claims.claim: When no match continues, a new match starts where the reverse pass marks the initial state, so the forward pass knows whether a longer match exists and never backtracks.

sources.label: search-step.ts, match starts
sources.quote: a match starts at j when reach[j][initial state]

sources.label: search-step.ts, no backtracking
sources.quote: never has to go back to where a longest match ended

claims.claim: On the text 'no error found', the reverse pass starts a match only at the e and the forward pass carries it through five letters, so five positions are marked. This is worked out by hand from the rules above and was not executed.

sources.label: search-step.ts, rules applied by hand
sources.quote: Code point j continues the match when reached[j][s] && reach[j][s] for some state s

claims.claim: Per position the two passes cost 240 operations at 8 states, 664 at 16 and 2,280 at 32, whatever the length of the text.

sources.label: search-step.ts, header
sources.quote: 240 operations at 8 states, whatever the number of positions

claims.claim: Over a full 512-position document the two passes cost 122,888 operations at 8 states and 1,167,392 at 32, and every value is an integer that 32-bit floats hold exactly.

sources.label: bit-emit.ts, exactness
sources.quote: FP32 then computes every one of them without rounding

claims.claim: The search reads the highlighter's display kinds, so a match of a string or key never crosses an escape or a key boundary.

sources.label: search-step.ts, searchable kinds
sources.quote: so no match of 'strings' or 'keys' crosses one

claims.claim: The first working search took 7.81, 68.8 and 945 ms at 8, 16 and 32 states for 100,000 documents, back to back.
At 32 states a pass has 1,025 table reads, and the shader holds 4,648 statements, each a separate 32-bit float operation in the first writer.

sources.label: lab/json-search README, one f32 statement per operation
sources.quote: with one f32 statement per operation

claims.claim: On October 14 a second code writer, bit-emit.ts, rewrote only the shader text; the search program as written did not change, and it is still weighted sums, ReGLU gates and index reads.

sources.label: lab/status.md, October 14 update
sources.quote: The search program as written didn't change

sources.label: lab/status.md, October 14 update
sources.quote: it is still weighted sums, ReGLU gates and index reads

claims.claim: When both inputs of a relu are known to be bits, relu(a minus b) is a AND the flip of b, so a subtraction and a clamp become one logic operation.

sources.label: bit-emit.ts, relu identity
sources.quote: E.g. relu(a - b) is `a & (b ^ 1u)`

claims.claim: A row of up to 32 states fits one 32-bit word, so a gate reading many table entries of one row becomes one AND of two words and a test against zero.

sources.label: lab/json-search README, one word per row
sources.quote: since a row of up to 32 states is one word there

sources.label: bit-emit.ts, word gate
sources.quote: (word[base] & opens) == 0u

claims.claim: The second writer packs a value into bits or integers only where the declared ranges prove it is a whole number; everywhere else it writes the same float statements.

sources.label: bit-emit.ts, what is proven
sources.quote: A value is "whole" when it is a whole number within a range inside ±2^24

sources.label: bit-emit.ts, fallback
sources.quote: Every other operation is written by emit.ts's row writer, as loop-emit.ts writes it

claims.claim: Back to back, at 8 states the search went from 7.81 to 4.60 ms and at 16 states from 68.8 to 4.72 ms, for 100,000 documents.
At 32 states the search went from 945 to 5.24 ms, which is 1.7, 15 and 180 times less across the three sizes.

sources.label: lab/json-search README, ratios
sources.quote: That is 1.7, 15 and 180 times less back to back.

claims.claim: Searches of 100 to 10,000 documents take 0.6 to 1.9 ms at any of the three pattern sizes, so the search no longer slows with the pattern's size.

sources.label: lab/json-search README, floor
sources.quote: 100 to 10,000 documents take 0.6 to 1.9 ms at any of the three sizes

claims.claim: Those times are back to back; a search after a pause of 200 ms or more takes 2.4 to 3.2 times the back-to-back time.

sources.label: lab/json-search README, after a pause
sources.quote: A search after a pause of 200 ms or more takes 2.4 to 3.2 times the back to back time

claims.claim: The searcher uses the bit writer for search and keeps the first writer for the highlighter, because the bit writer gave no gain for the highlighter's pass.

sources.quote: So the searcher keeps loop-emit.ts's shader for the highlighter.
